Then, when the night had turned to dawn, he was asked about his dream-vision.
Having heard it during the day, one should remain free from doubt, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious.
The Buddha-holder shall bring the seven royal families into harmony.
Then, my son, you must [maintain] the commitment and the restraint spoken by the Victorious One.
With faith, observe the command of your guru, and living beings must not be killed by you.
Those who desire accomplishment should not take what is not given, nor should they engage in sexual misconduct.
One should never drink intoxicants, nor should one ever eat meat and the like.
One should not perform what is harmful to sentient beings, nor should one abandon the Three Jewels.
The mudrā of the heart of bodhicitta, as well as the gurus and deities, are likewise [to be visualized].
Since the command of the guru is inviolable, it is he who can cause one to transcend even sin.
One should not step over discarded flower offerings (nirmālya), nor should one tread upon their shadow.
And likewise the forms of the mudrās.
One should not revile the deity of the mantra, nor should one perform rites for planetary spirits.
And one should not revile the followers of other paths.
In brief, one should not harbor doubt, hesitation, or uncertainty.
And likewise among the deities and others of one's own Tantra.
With firm faith, one should receive the empowerment from the Omniscient One exactly as prescribed.
The consecration of the ten [initiates] with the full set of jars and other implements may be performed according to one's wish.
Then, the vajra and bell should be placed in the hands.
Then, having taken the seven precious jewels, beginning with the wheel.
For the sake of attaining sovereignty, dominion, and the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
And one should perform the consecration for the shattering of evil.
One should cause the disciple who desires to accomplish the mantra to hear the command.
Then, having bowed with the head in faith, [he offered] whatever wealth was available.
It should be given to the teacher.
Jewels, treasuries, grain, silver, gold, vehicles, and houses.
Seats, boys, girls, men, and women are to be given.
And villages and cities according to their desires.
With clarity of one's own mind, one should cause the sacrificial fees to enter.
For the sake of swift accomplishment, one should offer even oneself in brief to the guru.
In this very life, there are all manner of pleasures without exception, and in the next world, there is the supreme bliss.
If even Buddhahood is attained [through this], how much more so the happiness of the gods?
By disparaging the Vajrācārya, who is equal to all the Buddhas.
Thinking, "This leads to the attainment of constant suffering," one should not revile the teacher.
A yogin should not revile his vajra-brother, sister, or mother.
And one should not harbor resentment.
One should not tolerate those who harm the Three Jewels.
Likewise, those who revile their guru, the wicked, and those who transgress their commitments (samaya).
And [one should avoid] those who perform such harmful acts as these.
In this way, one attains the accomplishment spoken of by the Omniscient One.
One who is compassionate toward all sentient beings attains swift accomplishment.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One spoke the ritual procedure for the sake of the welfare and happiness of the world of the gods, including Indra:
"On a cloth, one should likewise paint the Blessed One, the All-Knowing One;
and on the right, the Tathāgata Sarvadurgatipariśodhanarāja."
To the left is Śākyamuni;
below the Sarvadurgatipariśodhana is Āryāvalokiteśvara, with the color of the moon and sun, holding a lotus in his hand;
and below Śākyamuni is Vajrapāṇi.
Between those two, one should paint Bhaiṣajyarāja, blue in color, holding a *hāritakī* fruit in one hand and making the gesture of granting boons (*varada*) with the other;
and Hayagrīva and Trailokyavijaya, intent on subduing the wicked, facing their respective deities.
Between those two, one should paint Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍuravāsinī, and Tārā, each holding her own characteristic emblem in her hands.
Below them, one should draw a lotus pond filled with various water-born flowers and containing crocodiles, fish, white frogs, and so forth.
One should also draw incense, lamps, perfumes, garlands, food offerings, and various kinds of flowers and fruits.
And below that, one should draw the practitioner seated, bowing with palms joined in *añjali*.
Then, relying upon the empowerment of the truth of the cloth-painting, one should open one's eyes and perform worship.
Thereafter, if one perceives a sign, success will be attained quickly;
if one does not perceive it, success will be attained after a long time.
One should also [employ] the sound of laughter, the word "karma," and the resonance of the ringing bell.
And having seen the monks, the brahmin girls, and the fruits, he quickly [acted].
Success is achieved in the highest, middling, and lowest accomplishments.
Then, one should consecrate the cloth-painting with mantras and mudrās.
And having sat down before him, one should worship with whatever has been obtained.
Having performed the protection of oneself and so forth with the Trailokyavijaya [mantra].
And having meditated upon the reality of the self.
One should recite the mantra either three hundred thousand or six hundred thousand times, until the signs of accomplishment have appeared.
Then, staying in a secluded place, one should complete eight hundred recitations,
reciting the mantra neither deficiently nor redundantly.
Then, at the conclusion of the recitation, having visualized the maṇḍala as before and performed an extensive worship, one should recite for one night.
Then, if he beholds the Pradhāna, his son, and the deities,
he should request the supreme accomplishment desired according to his capacity;
the deities, being eternally pleased, grant him the fruit of accomplishment.
Having paid homage, one should receive the supreme accomplishment and so forth;
having bestowed the nature of the Guru and the Three Jewels,
the wise one should then always conduct himself among those who lack them.
Having taken it up, one should practice it oneself;
being a benefactor to all sentient beings, one shall remain for many eons. Even if not fully accomplished, it will become a performer of all rites.
Yakṣas, constellations, planets, and the like become performers of all rites, such as those for pacification, at the mere word [of the practitioner], acting like servants.
Then, indeed, Devendra said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, how should one proceed for the sake of eliminating the sufferings of hell and so forth for those beings who are evildoers and have fallen under the power of the hells and other realms?"
The Blessed One said:
"O Lord of Devas, listen! Hear how those beings who have fallen under the power of hell and committed great evils may be liberated from the sufferings of hell without effort.
In that same manner, having drawn the mandala, one should perform the consecration as before with water-pots over which the mantra has been recited one hundred and eight times."
Thereupon, having been freed from all sins, they are swiftly liberated from all the sufferings of the hells and other realms.
Those great-souled ones, their sins now liberated, are reborn among the Śuddhāvāsa deities,
where they constantly participate in the communal recitation of the Buddha’s Dharma.
And those established on the stage of non-retrogression gradually realize awakening;
or else, having written its image or its name with saffron, [they do so].
For the sake of liberating sentient beings from the great fear of the three lower realms.
The minister, devoted to the welfare of others, should consecrate [the disciple] with compassion.
Then that yogin should perform the consecration with mantras and mudrās.
Having fashioned the form of the deity, one should place it within the shrine.
Having written the heart-mantra of one's own deity and that of the other deity in the region of their respective hearts.
Having generated a mind equal to that of a deity, one may dwell at home.
And having analyzed that name, one should write the mantra with saffron.
One should perform the work for the caitya until one hundred thousand [recitations] are completed.
For the destruction of the sins of a great sinner, one should complete even ten million [recitations].
When this has been done, they will certainly be liberated from hell.
Likewise, having been liberated from the animal realm, they are reborn among the classes of gods.
Having analyzed that name, one should recite the aforementioned mantra one thousand times.
At times he might even fulfill a hundred thousand, up to fulfilling even ten million.
They are reborn among the classes of gods.
Having analyzed that name, one who is skilled [should recite it] a hundred thousand times, or even up to a million.
One should perform the fire oblation; they become liberated from the sins that lead to the great hells.
Until a sign arises in the place of the blazing fire.
Sesame seeds, white mustard seeds, and rice grains mixed with goat's milk.
Furthermore, fuel-sticks smeared with fragrant substances should be offered according to the prescribed rule.
Then, having certainly been reborn among the hosts of gods, they manifest signs:
sometimes the appearance of supreme deities, or else within the center of the fire-pit, white, clockwise-turning flames that blaze upward, stainless and rising;
or a flame that is scattered yet continuous, stainless and steady like lightning.
He sees these signs of fire;
then they likewise manifest themselves as the nature of Vaiśvānara,
stainless like the moon, with a radiant complexion and a blazing face.
From observing these signs, one should understand their liberation from hell and other realms, the shattering of their sins, and their rebirth in heaven;
furthermore, one should dig a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring four cubits according to the prescribed rules.
On the perimeter, one should draw a circle of vajras, and in the center, a wheel.
One should draw the mudrās of the five families as they truly are in their respective directions.
Likewise, one should draw the Lord of the World together with the sentient beings.
Therefore, there are full water-jars and vessels filled with sacrificial offerings.
Eight or sixteen [seats] should be established, along with offerings of food and drink;
likewise, one should properly adorn [the site] with flower garlands and the like, as well as canopies, banners, cloths, and excellent parasols.
In this manner, one who knows the ritual procedure should offer oblations correctly into the supreme homa-pit; having thus written [the mantra], he should summon the host of deities.
One who knows the mantra should offer the *argha* with the mantra and mudrā.
Having performed the worship in brief, one who is attended by hosts of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas,
adorned with camphor, sandalwood, saffron, garments, and ornaments, should burn consecrated incense.
One should worship with flower garlands and other offerings;
likewise, having written the mantra on the crest and the arm, one should bind it there.
One should establish the presiding presence of all vidyās in the regions of the heart, throat, and mouth.

One should thus place the auspicious mantra-syllables on the forehead, the two eyebrows, the two ears, the head, the topknot, the two arms, the nose, the hips, the knees, the feet, the tip of the nose, the two eyes, the region of the private organ, and likewise on other parts as well.
Then, one should place the Durgatipariśodhana [mandala] together with its seat in the center of that;
thereafter, the mantra-practitioner should cover it with a consecrated cloth;
then, having properly kindled the fire.
O Sahasrajvālya!
Having drawn forth the peaceful and infinite fire, whose body is filled with a thousand flames and which resembles the moon within a sacrificial pit, one should offer the *argha* oblation.
In the same manner, the wise practitioner should place an image or other representation before him.
Having likewise invited the assembly of Tathāgatas, one should offer the water for honor (*argha*) and so forth, and perform the aforementioned worship in the same manner.
Then, having prepared the oblation (*āhuti*) and the sacrificial offering (*havya*), one should offer it to the Fire and recite the *Jinādinī* mantra one hundred and eight times.
Thereafter, one should offer twenty-one oblations with the King of Purification Mantras.
Then, having drawn Śvetamukha [into the mandala], one should worship him three times with ritual implements or with offerings such as the *argha*.

One should visualize or draw Vajrapāṇi, who holds a lotus-noose, whose form is that of the three worlds, who tramples sin under his lotus feet, who is adorned with all ornaments, and who wears the crown of the Perfectly Awakened Ones (*saṃbuddha*). Then, with his heart-mantra, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) one hundred thousand times, or even up to ten million (*koṭi*) times.
When the sign has arisen, the abandonment of the succession of evil should be understood in the same way.
Then, one should collect [the remains] according to the ritual procedure, reduced to ashes by means of the Vajrasaṃhāra mantra.

Having recited the purification mantra one hundred thousand times over ashes and bone fragments mixed with scented water and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should form them into a mass, mix it with camphor and fragrant earth, and fashion an image or a deity of a *caitya*.
This should be done either once, twice, thrice, four times, five times, or one hundred and eight times.
Having empowered it with mantras and mudrās, one should recite [the mantra] two hundred thousand times.
Then either the shrine blazes or the image laughs.
One smells the fragrance of incense and sees various kinds of gods and other beings; the miraculous powers (ṛddhiprātihārya) of the deity manifest, and flowers and other offerings fall.
Furthermore, the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, flutes, lutes, and so forth are heard.
If, due to an abundance of evil, one does not at times see these divine signs, then one should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times.
This continues until one has made an offering to the Tathāgata as a sign.
One who knows the ritual should recite while well-composed;
then at the end, one should recite for one night. At that time, his soul purified of evil, he will certainly see [the deity].
One thoroughly understands that continuum as the form-body of the deity.
Having recognized these signs with a non-conceptual mind,
one should perform all activities while being permeated by loving-kindness and compassion.
Even if it is not possible in this way, then one should write down its name alone and construct a garland of shrines (caityamālā) or fashion an image;
when the fire-oblation (homa) and consecration (abhiṣeka) have been performed,
they will certainly be reborn in the heavens.
Having empowered ashes, mustard seeds, sand, and so forth by reciting the name [of the person] over them, one should cast them into a river that flows to the ocean.
Thereby, even one who is most sinful will be liberated from the miserable states of existence (*durgati*).

For the meritorious world—having produced the supreme seeds of virtue, endowed with the fruit of Buddhahood, and manifested through the causes of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom—the miserable states of existence are shattered.
What need is there to speak further?

There is no doubt in this matter regarding one who has not produced roots of virtue, who holds nihilistic views, who has turned back from the path to awakening, who hates the teaching, who is harmful, who is ignorant of evil, whose heart is hostile toward mother and father, and who kills those who have renounced passion and have set their minds upon the thought of awakening.

The Sugatas, the Victors, have declared that for those who hold views such as the non-existence of the deities, the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, mantras, mudrās, and so forth, as well as for those most wicked ones, there is no liberation in the absence of wisdom and skillful means.
Then Śakra and the others, their eyes like blue and red lotuses, expressed their approval, saying, "Excellent!"

Having satisfied him, they worshipped him. And by Śakra, who delights in the welfare of others, it was requested as follows: "The Bestower of Boons should be depicted with a second [hand] holding a three-pronged vajra; with one left hand he holds a trident, and with the second he holds a sword; his sacred thread is a snake, and his throat is blue. Thus he should be painted.
Oṃ paśupati nīlakaṇṭha umāpriya svāhā!
Now follows its mudrā:

having formed a left fist with the right hand, one should press the little finger with the thumb; having made the remaining fingers have the characteristics of a vajra, one should slightly bend the ring finger and the index finger into the shape of a vajra.
This is the mudrā of Paśupati.
Viṣṇu is mounted upon Garuḍa, black in color, and four-armed;
with his two right arms, he holds a mace and a thunderbolt.
He holds a conch and a discus in his two left hands;
Vajrahemā is golden-colored, with a seat, arms, and weapons like Viṣṇu.
[Vajravārāhī] is red in color, has six faces, is mounted upon a peacock holding a vajra-bell, and holds a spear and a vajra in her two right hands.
With his two left hands, he holds a cock, a bell, and a vajra;
Vajrakaumārī should be understood as holding a vajra and a bell in exactly the same manner.
Maunavajra is mounted upon a swan, is golden in color, and has four faces; with his two right arms, he holds a vajra and a rosary.
Holding a staff and a water-pot in his two left hands, Vajraśānti is to be known as being like Brahmā.
Vajrāyudha is white-complexioned and mounted upon a white elephant; he holds a crossed-vajra (viśvavajra) in his left hand and a supramundane vajra in his right hand.
Vajramuṣṭi is to be known as being like Vajrāyudha.

The wrathful deity Vajrakuṇḍalī is mounted upon a chariot; he is red in color, holds a vajra with his right hand together with a lotus, and holds a solar disc with his left hand together with a lotus.
Vajrāmṛtā is exactly like the wrathful deity Vajrakuṇḍalī.
The wrathful Vajraprabha is white in color, mounted upon a swan; he holds a vajra in his right hand and a lotus with a moon in his left.
Vajrakānti is like Vajraprabha.
The wrathful Vajradaṇḍa is mounted upon a tortoise, blue in color, holding a vajra in his right hand and a staff (*daṇḍa*) in his left.
Daṇḍavajrāgrī is like Vajradaṇḍakrodha.
The wrathful Vajrapiṅgala is mounted upon a goat, red in color, holding a vajra in his right hand and, with his left, holding and devouring a human being as he stands.
Vajramekhalā is like Vajrapiṅgala-krodha.
Vajraśauṇḍa is Gaṇapati, who rides an elephant; he stands holding a vajra in his right hand and a plow in his left, and is white in color.
Vajraviṇayā is like Vajraśauṇḍa, with this distinction: namely, she holds a *khaṭvāṅga* in her left hand.
Gaṇapati is Vajramāla, green in color, mounted upon a chariot drawn by cuckoos; he holds a vajra in his right hand and a garland of flowers in his left.
Vajrāsanā is like Vajramālā, with this distinction: namely, she holds a spear (*śakti*) in her left hand.

Vajravaśī is mounted on a boar-chariot, fair-complexioned, holding a vajra in his right hand and a dolphin-banner in his left. Vajravaśā is like Vajravaśī, with this distinction, namely that she is red in color.
Vijayavajra is Gaṇapati, mounted on a frog, white in color, holding a vajra in his right hand and a sword in his left.
Vajrasenā is like Vijayavajrā.
Vajramusala is the messenger; he is mounted upon a flower-palace, fair in complexion, holding a vajra in his right hand and a mallet (*musala*) in his left.
Vajradūtī is like Vajramusala, with this distinction: that she holds a *khaṭvāṅga* in her left hand.
Vajrāniladūta is blue in color, mounted on a deer; he holds a vajra in his right hand and a cloth in his left.
Vegavajriṇī is like Vajrāniladūta.

Vajrānaladūta is red in color, mounted on a goat, with the radiance of upward-flaming light and three-crested flames; he holds a vajra and armor in his two right arms, and a staff and a water-pot in his two left arms.
Vajrajvālā is like a vajra-fire.
Vajrabhairavadūta is blue, mounted upon a vetāla, holding a vajra in his right hand and a mace in his left.
The messenger Vajravikaṭā is like Vajrabhairava; however, her distinction is this: she holds a noose in her left hand.
The servant Vajrāṅkuśa is blue, has the face of a boar, and rides upon the serpent Śeṣa;
he holds a vajra in his right hand and an ankusha in his left.

The maidservant Vajramukhī is blue in color, mounted on a man; she has the face of a boar, holds a vajra in her right hand, and a sword in her left. The maidservant Vajrakāla is dark blue, mounted on a buffalo; he holds a vajra in his right hand and the staff of Yama (yamadaṇḍa) in his left. The maidservant Vajrakālī is black in color, mounted on a vetāla; she holds a khaṭvāṅga in her left hand and a vajra in her right hand.
Vajravināyakaceṭaka is mounted upon a rat, white in color, and elephant-faced; with his two right hands he holds a vajra and an axe, and with his two left hands he holds a trident and a staff.
He has a snake as his sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
Vajrapūtanā is a female servant (*ceṭī*) who is blue in color; she holds a vajra in her right hand and a broom in her left.
Undurārūḍhā; Nāgavajraceṭaka is mounted upon a crocodile, has eight hoods, is white in color, holds a vajra in his right hand and a nāga-noose in his left;
Vajramakarā is a female servant (ceṭī) mounted upon a crocodile and is white in color.
She has eight hoods;
with her right hand she holds a vajra, and with her left she holds a makara marked with a vajra.
Bhīmā is dark blue in color; with her right hand she holds a vajra, and with her left she holds a sword and a phetkāra-staff.
Śrī Gauravarṇā holds a vajra in her right hand and a lotus in her left;
Sarasvatī holds a lute in her hands, with a vajra in her left and [a lute] in her right.
Durgā is dark blue in color, mounted upon a lion, holding a vajra and a wheel in her two right hands, and a paṭṭiśa and a conch in her two left hands.
Regarding all the Mothers and the deities from Rudra down to Varuṇa, it should be understood that the vajra mentioned as being held in their right hands is one with three prongs.
Furthermore, all worldly and supramundane deities are to be depicted facing Vairocana.

Then, when the time of twilight has arrived, having bound the *vajraterintirī* [headband] and taken a garland of blue flowers, one should enter the mandala while uttering the four *huṃ*s. One should perform seven circumambulations of Vajravairocana while sounding the conch, the vajra, and the bell.
Having gazed upon the entire mandala for the sake of pacifying any defects of deficiency or excess, and having offered the garland to the Blessed One and performed the vajra-dance;
Having taken [it], one should bind it to one's own head with the four *huṃ* syllables alone;
likewise, one should complete whatever is deficient according to what has been stated.
The Buddha would abandon what is excessive; he would cause the vajra-bell to ring.
"It is accomplished and no fault is incurred.
Then, standing in the center, the Vajrācārya becomes absorbed in meditative concentration.
And with the mind, one should open the four vajra gates.
Oṃ, open the vajra! Enter the samaya! Hūṃ! And its mudrā is as follows:
firmly holding the tips of two vajra-fingers together, with the palms facing upward.
Being well-enraged, one should perform the supreme opening of the door.
Thus,

having performed the ritual actions with the hook and other implements, [one should prepare] a flask made of the seven precious gems, or one made of clay, which has its mouth facing downward, a high neck, drooping lips, and a large belly, and is filled with divine scented water.

It is filled with all kinds of jewels, medicinal herbs, and grains; it is laden with fruit and foliage, its neck bound with fine cloth, and protected on all sides externally by divine perfumes. It is adorned with garlands, marked with a vajra, and surmounted by a great vajra empowered by the *krodha-terintirī* who grasps a vajra-flower vine.

Having consecrated [the water] one thousand and eight times with "Oṃ vajrodaka hūṃ" and having consecrated it one hundred and eight times with the four *huṃ* syllables, one should place it before the Blessed One Vajrahuṃkāra.
Then, one should place a second flask outside, facing the entrance door, having recited the four *huṃ* syllables over it one hundred and eight times.
Having performed the self-consecration and the consecration of the disciples with that water, [one proceeds].
Having formed the *praveśamudrā*, one should either bind [the mantra] or not.
Coral, gold, conch, pearl, and gem,
as well as all precious gems, and the medicinal herbs *siṃhī*, *vyāghrī*, *girikarṇī*, and *sahadevā*— these are all the medicinal plants.
One should indicate those five— sesame, mung beans, barley, grain, and wheat as the fifth—
as representing all types of rice by means of their names.
Then, after having them undertake the vows preceded by the four prostrations and so forth, one should recite the mantra over blue garments with the Vajrayakṣa mantra.

The preceptor, having donned the garment with the *sattvoṣṇīṣa*, the face-covering with the gatekeepers, and the upper robe with the *vajrakavaca*, and having bound on the *uṣṇīṣa* and other ornaments, takes blue flowers with the *krodhaterintī* mantra. Reciting "Oṃ, I enter the *vajrasamaya*," he enters and makes a formal request to all the Tathāgatas.
With the words "I, O Blessed One," and so forth,

one then drinks the vajra-water, performs the self-entry (*ātmāveśa*), casts that garland into the great mandala, binds it upon one's own head, removes the blindfold, and, having beheld the mandala as it truly is, performs the release from the entry-mudrā with the words "Stay, O Vajra," and so forth.

Having prostrated to the Blessed One and received from the Blessed One the water consecration, the crown of the five Buddhas, the silk ribbon, the vajra garland, and the vajra-name consecration of the Lord;
Having taken up the reality (tattva), the commitment of the Dharma (dharmasamaya), and the vow of the Vajra of Accomplishment (siddhivajravrata);
having worshipped oneself with flowers and the like, as well as with the gestures of grace (lāsya) and so forth;

having received permission by means of the five verses and the prophecy of the *udgata-huṃkāra*; and having again performed the self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) and so on, one should perform recitation according to one's preference, thinking: "I am the Vajra of Huṃ, I am the Vajra of Huṃ."
Having uttered his own name with "I am," and having bound the great mudrā of Vairocana,
he should cause himself to enter into the Tathāgata-vajra at the place of Vairocana by means of that mantra ending in the syllable *Aḥ*.
Having visualized the vajra-egoity, thinking "I am the Vajra," one should meditate on that vajra as Vairocana,
thinking "I am the Vajra-realm."

In this manner, up until having bound the great mudrā of the Vajra-entrance (*vajrāveśa-mahāmudrā*) at the northern gate, one should cause oneself to enter [the state] by means of its mantra ending with the syllable *āḥ*. Having generated the ego-identity (*ahaṃkāra*), "I am the Vajra-bell," one should meditate, "I am the Wrathful One of Vajra-entrance. In this way, it is accomplished by means of the vajra.
Then, having bound the Sattva-vajrāṅkuśī mudrā, the Vajra-ācārya, performing the clapping of hands once again, should assemble all the Buddhas.
Oṃ vajrasamāja jaḥ vaṃ hoḥ. One should recite this twenty-one times.
Then, one should quickly utter the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of the Vajra Wrath Samaya.
Having recited the eight names one hundred times for a single session— the most excellent [practice]— one should then,

by means of the vajra-hook and other implements through their respective doors, attract, cause to enter, bind, and subjugate [the deities]. Having offered the *argha* as prescribed with the four *huṃ* syllables,
one should accomplish Śrī Vairocana and the others, up to those of the Bhadrakalpa, by means of the samaya-mudrās.
Having recited one's own mantra, one should say:

Then, by reciting one's own mantra, they indeed become accomplished.

I shall cause the disciples to enter for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
And in this entry into the mandala, no examination of whether one is a worthy vessel or not should be performed.
Why is that?
Venerable sir, there are certain beings who have committed great sins; yet, upon seeing and entering this Vajra-hūṃkāra mandala, they shall become free from all states of woe.

There are, O Blessed Ones, beings who are greedy for all objects of enjoyment, food, and the qualities of desire; who are hostile to the *samaya*; and who are incapable of performing the preliminary practices (*puraścaraṇa*) and so forth. For them as well, having entered here, there shall be the fulfillment of all hopes according to their wishes, as they act as they please.

And there are, O Blessed Ones, beings who, out of a fondness for dancing, singing, laughter, performance, food, and recreation, and due to their lack of realization of the Mahāyāna reality of all Tathāgatas, enter the maṇḍalas of other deities;
yet, fearing the precepts, they do not enter the maṇḍalas of all Tathāgata families—which are the means of gathering all hopes, fulfilling them, and producing unsurpassed delight, joy, and gladness.
For them, rather than entering the maṇḍalas of the lower realms, it is appropriate that they enter the Vajra-hūṃkāra maṇḍala, which is the very samaya of bliss and self as it truly exists.
